routes.description: Establish that Jesus personally claimed divine identity by reading his titles, sayings, prerogatives, and reception cumulatively within a first-century Jewish two-powers framework and by defending that interpretation against delegated-authority alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the relevant Jewish framework can include distinguishable divine figures, Jesus applies that identity framework to himself through words and functions, and the cumulative evidence is not adequately explained by mere agency, exalted humanity, or later attribution.

motionBridge.description: Connect Jesus's own claimed titles, authority, and functions to personal participation in divine identity rather than merely to later beliefs about him.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Jewish scripture supplied a recognizable framework of distinguishable figures sharing Yahweh's identity and that Jesus located himself within it.
Show that Jesus's Son, Lord, Son of Man, divine-name, unity, and preexistence language communicates more than messianic or representative status.
Show that Jesus's claims to equal honor, universal judgment, life-giving authority, resurrection power, and premundane glory identify him with divine functions.
Connect followers' devotion and opponents' accusations to Jesus's self-claims while establishing that the resulting high christology is early rather than a late development.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how receiving authority, serving, and distinguishing himself from the Father can coexist with prior divine identity through incarnation and exaltation.
Establish when worship language and hostile reactions reliably corroborate the intended force of Jesus's claims.

routes.description: Defeat the claim that Jesus personally identified himself as God by showing that the cited language, functions, and honors remain explicable through divine name-bearing, delegated agency, messianic or ideal-human status, and later high christology.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative cannot bridge from disputed texts and received authority to Jesus's own divine identity because viable agency readings remain, contrary dependence language persists, or early Christian portrayals do not establish Jesus's historical self-claim.

motionBridge.description: Show that exalted status, divine authorization, name-bearing, or later portrayal does not by itself establish that Jesus personally claimed to be God.

centralBridges.description: Establish that Jewish representatives could bear God's name, exercise transmitted authority, and receive deference without being identical with Yahweh.
Show that unity, glory, judgment, forgiveness, miraculous power, and other assertedly divine features are received by Jesus or extended to disciples.
Provide non-divine readings of the principal Johannine, Synoptic, Danielic, and Pauline terms and passages used to infer divine identity.
Separate claims made by Jesus from followers' devotion, authorial framing, later high christology, and historically disputed interpretations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show that blasphemy accusations, stoning attempts, and other reactions may reflect misunderstanding or charges that do not require a divine-identity claim.
Distinguish homage language applicable to non-divine recipients from cultic service that would uniquely identify its recipient as God.

sections.title: Two powers, divine name-bearing, and Jewish agency
sections.rationale: This issue supplies the controlling historical framework for deciding whether distinguishable Yahweh figures and divine name-bearing imply shared divine identity or delegated representation.

sections.title: Jesus's sayings, titles, and scriptural allusions
sections.rationale: The motion centrally depends on whether Son, Lord, Son of Man, unity, preexistence, and divine-name language constitutes Jesus's personal divine claim or permits non-divine readings.

sections.title: Divine prerogatives, dependence, and delegated authority
sections.rationale: Claims involving judgment, resurrection, life, forgiveness, glory, and Sabbath authority must be tested against language of receipt, dependence, prayer, and comparable grants to disciples.

sections.title: Worship, early devotion, and hostile reactions
sections.rationale: Followers' prayers and homage and opponents' blasphemy reactions may corroborate Jesus's intended claim, but their semantic force and reliability require independent assessment.

sections.title: Historical self-claim and christological development
sections.rationale: The debate requires separating Jesus's own claims from Gospel framing and early Christian christology while assessing Synoptic and Johannine differences, Pauline material, and proposed development.

chunk-001:c002.proposition: Old Testament portrayals of two distinguishishable figures acting as Yahweh establish a two-powers framework within which Jesus identifies himself as one divine power.

chunk-001:c004.proposition: Jesus presents himself as the unique Son, David's heavenly Lord, and Daniel's cloud-riding Son of Man, thereby claiming the identity of a heavenly divine power.

chunk-001:c005.proposition: Jesus claims divine status by assuming Yahweh's roles as universal judge and raiser of the dead while requiring honor equal to the Father's.

chunk-001:c006.proposition: The earliest Christians treated Jesus as divine Lord and creative Word, applied Yahweh's name and honors to him, and directed worship, prayer, hymns, baptism, and liturgy toward him.

chunk-002:c002-04.proposition: Scriptural interaction between Yahweh and the angel of Yahweh supports two distinguishable heavenly powers rather than reducing the angel to a merely delegated human representative.

chunk-002:c002-07.proposition: Stephen's vision and prayer to Jesus, together with the earliest Christians calling on Jesus's name, show Jesus receiving Yahweh-associated devotion within roughly two years of the crucifixion.

chunk-003:c003-06.proposition: Philippians 2 depicts a preexistent divine being who voluntarily assumes human likeness and receives universal homage, rather than an ordinary image-bearing human elevated only afterward.

chunk-003:c003-07.proposition: Jesus's use of the Septuagint's doubled Kyrios formula points to Yahweh and, alongside the shared conclusions of followers and enemies, supports an intentionally veiled but genuine divine claim.

chunk-004:c004-04.proposition: Jesus's receipt of authority is compatible with prior divine identity because the divine Son assumes servant status in incarnation and is subsequently exalted, as reflected across Daniel 7, Philippians 2, John 1, and Matthew.

chunk-005:c005-03.proposition: Different authorial emphases explain the Synoptics' omission of Johannine-style sayings, while Mark's progressive disclosure and Paul's early material show that divine christology was neither uniquely Johannine nor necessarily late.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: Jesus's appeal to Psalm 82 answers the charge of claiming deity by comparing his title with non-Yahweh beings called gods and by identifying himself as God's consecrated and sent Son.

chunk-001:c009.proposition: Even if Jesus's 'I am' language evokes Exodus, Jewish traditions permit a non-Yahweh representative to bear God's name and exercise God's authority, so name-bearing does not establish identity with Yahweh.

chunk-002:c002-01.proposition: John 8:58 can present Jesus as the fulfillment eternally planned in Abraham's promised redemption rather than asserting Jesus's personal preexistence or identity with Yahweh.

chunk-002:c002-02.proposition: An attempt to stone Jesus does not establish that his opponents correctly understood him as claiming deity, because Johannine opponents repeatedly misunderstand him and blasphemy accusations can arise from broader alleged offenses.

chunk-002:c002-10.proposition: Jesus receives and then delegates glory, judgment, and forgiveness, showing that possession of these allegedly divine prerogatives can reflect transmitted authority rather than personal identity as God.

chunk-003:c003-01.proposition: The Gospels' pervasive misunderstanding and the Synoptic messianic-secret motif make it difficult to treat the record as evidence that Jesus clearly and publicly communicated a personal claim to be God.

chunk-003:c003-03.proposition: Jesus's acceptance of proskynesis does not establish deity because the term can denote bodily homage to human authorities, whereas the New Testament uses distinct language for cultic service reserved for God.

chunk-004:c004-03.proposition: John 5 describes the Son's life-giving and judicial authority as granted or entrusted by the Father, indicating received and dependent authority rather than powers necessarily possessed through divine identity.

chunk-004:c004-08.proposition: The lack of early literary evidence for a two-powers controversy weakens the claim that a settled first-century two-powers framework governed how Jesus's hearers would interpret divine figures or his trial language.

chunk-005:c005-04.proposition: Even granting that Paul held a high christology does not establish that Jesus personally claimed to be God, because Pauline interpretation remains distinct from the historical question of Jesus's own self-understanding.
